---
title: "Setup"
---

You will need two things for this class: **R** and **Positron**. Git is optional but worth having.

Do this before the first discussion section. The first section walks through installation, but it goes much better if you arrive with something already working.

Positron is Posit's data science IDE — the same people who make RStudio. If you have used RStudio before, everything you know transfers: the console, scripts, plots and variables are all still there, laid out a little differently.

---

## Install in this order

The order matters. Positron does not install R and does not warn you about it.

### 1. R

Download from [cloud.r-project.org](https://cloud.r-project.org/). Take the build that matches your machine — Apple Silicon Macs need the `arm64` package, not the Intel one. Accept the defaults.

Verify: open R and check that it prints a version number of **4.2 or above**. Positron supports 4.2 and higher only; it will find older installations and then discard them, which looks like R is missing when it is merely too old.

### 2. Positron

Download from [positron.posit.co/download.html](https://positron.posit.co/download.html). It is free.

- **macOS** — requires macOS 11 or later. Take the Apple Silicon build on an M-series Mac, the Intel build otherwise.
- **Windows** — take the **User install** unless you have administrator rights and want it available to everyone on the machine. Windows also needs the latest Visual C++ Redistributable, which most machines already have.

**Install R first.** Positron finds R by itself — on macOS it looks in `/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions` and on your `PATH`; on Windows it checks `Program Files\R`, `AppData\Local\Programs\R`, and the registry. With no R installed there is nothing to find, and Positron opens with no R session, which looks like Positron is broken. It is not. Install R, then reopen Positron.

If R is installed and the Console still does not start one, use the interpreter picker at the top of the Console (**Select Interpreter**) and choose your R version.

### 3. Do not install Quarto

**Positron already includes Quarto.** Plenty of tutorials open by telling you to download Quarto separately. You do not need to. A separate install can end up ahead of or behind the one Positron uses, and then two machines that look identical behave differently.

### 4. The tidyverse

In the Positron **Console**:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")
```

This is one command that installs about thirty packages, so it takes a few minutes and prints a great deal of output. That is normal.

If R asks whether to use a **personal library**, say yes. On a new machine the system-wide library is usually not writable, and without a personal library the install fails with `unable to install packages` — which reads like a network problem but is a permissions one.

You install a package **once per machine** and load it **once per session**:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse")   # once per computer; note the quotes
library(tidyverse)              # once per session; no quotes
```

This distinction trips up everyone at first. `install.packages()` buys the book; `library()` takes it off the shelf. When you see `could not find function "read_csv"`, the diagnosis is almost always a missing `library(tidyverse)` at the top of your script.

Loading the tidyverse prints a list of attached packages and a couple of "conflicts." Also normal, also not an error.

### 5. Git — optional

You do not need Git to take this course. Everything here can be downloaded from GitHub with the green **Code** button and **Download ZIP**.

Git is worth having anyway, because it means one command brings you every new week's materials instead of re-downloading. If you want it:

- **macOS**: run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal and click through the dialog.
- **Windows**: [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win). The installer asks a great many questions and the defaults are fine.
- **Linux**: `sudo apt install git`

Then clone this repository once:

```
git clone https://github.com/govt6019/website.git
```

After that, `git pull` from inside the folder brings you every new week's materials.

---

## Check that it works

In the Positron Console:

```r
# Version 4.2 or above?
R.version.string

# Packages load?
library(tidyverse)

# Can you read the course dataset?
voter <- read_csv("data/voter2012.csv")
dim(voter)
```

That last one depends on where you are working from. If it fails with a message about the file not existing, the problem is almost never the file — it is that R is looking somewhere else. `getwd()` tells you where R currently is. Section 1 covers this properly.

Then, visually: make a new file, save it with a `.qmd` extension, put one R chunk in it, and click **Preview** in the editor's action bar. Check that you get an HTML page out.

---

## When something breaks

**Restart R.** Use the restart button in the Console's action bar, or open the Command Palette (`Cmd+Shift+P` on macOS, `Ctrl+Shift+P` on Windows) and run **Restart Active Interpreter Session**. This fixes a surprising amount and does not lose your script. Restarting fresh and running your code from the top is the single most useful debugging move you have.

Read the error message before anything else. Most R errors name the function that failed and the thing it could not find, and that is usually the whole diagnosis.

If you are stuck for more than twenty minutes, stop and bring it to section or office hours. Do not lose an evening to an install problem.
